text: Rosemarie Trockel, born on 13 November 1952 in Schwerte, Nordrhein-Westfalen, West Germany, is a German conceptual artist known for her work in drawings, paintings, sculptures, videos, installations, and mixed media. From 1985, she began creating large-scale paintings using industrial knitting machines, which often featured geometric motifs, logos such as the Playboy Bunny or a hammer and sickle, and the phrase "Made in West Germany." Between 1974 and 1978, she studied anthropology, mathematics, sociology, and theology while attending the Werkkunstschule in Cologne, a period marked by the strong influence of Joseph Beuys. In the early 1980s, she met members of the Mülheimer Freiheit artist group, founded by Jiří Georg Dokoupil and Walter Dahn, and exhibited at the women-only gallery of Monika Sprüth in Cologne. Her work frequently critiques other artists or artistic styles, such as minimal art. During the 1980s, she also contributed to the magazine Eau de Cologne, which focused on women artists. In 1994, she created the Frankfurter Engel monument for Frankfurt. For Documenta in 1997, she collaborated with Carsten Höller on an installation in one of the exhibition's outbuildings. Since the late 1990s, she has worked extensively with clay and continued producing both hand and machine knitted "paintings," several of which were shown in the 2005 retrospective Post-Menopause at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne. In 2013, her work was included in the Italian Pavilion, and she represented Germany at the Venice Biennale in 1999; she also participated in Documenta in 1997 and 2012. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she collaborated with Bottega Veneta designer Daniel Lee on the brand’s 2021 ad campaign. Trockel is a professor at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in Düsseldorf, Nordrhein-Westfalen, and her students have included Tea Jorjadze, Michail Pirgelis, and Bettina Pousttchi. She has been represented by Sprüth Magers and Gladstone.
